questions.title: The second derivative that changes sign at two points
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.7 (the second derivative; concavity and points of inflection)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The function is engineered so the second derivative is a quadratic with two distinct real roots, forcing the student to test three separate intervals rather than assume a single inflection point.
questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=x^{4}-8x^{3}+18x^{2}$. You are to analyse its concavity using the second derivative.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $f''(x)=12x^{2}-48x+36$ and that this factorises as $12(x-1)(x-3)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the values of $x$ for which $f''(x)=0$, and state why these are the only candidates for a change of concavity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine whether the curve is convex or concave on each of the intervals $x<1$, $1<x<3$ and $x>3$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that $x=1$ and $x=3$ are both points of inflection.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Begin by differentiating the polynomial $f(x)=x^{4}-8x^{3}+18x^{2}$ once with respect to $x$ to obtain $f'(x)=4x^{3}-24x^{2}+36x$ **(M1)**, then differentiate this result a second time to obtain $f''(x)=12x^{2}-48x+36$ **(A1)**. The quadratic $x^{2}-4x+3$ factors as $(x-1)(x-3)$, so $f''(x)=12(x-1)(x-3)$ **(A1)(AG)**. This confirms the given form, because multiplying the brackets back together restores $12x^{2}-48x+36$ exactly, leaving no remainder, and this step underpins every later part.

**(b)** Concavity can only change where the second derivative vanishes, so solve $12(x-1)(x-3)=0$ **(M1)**. A product of real factors is zero precisely when one factor is zero, giving $x-1=0$ or $x-3=0$, thus $x=1$ and $x=3$ **(A1)**. These two values are the only real roots of the quadratic, so they form the complete set of candidates that must be tested for a sign change before any conclusion is drawn.

**(c)** Choose one convenient test value inside each of the three intervals. At $x=0$ we have $f''(0)=36>0$, so the curve is convex on $x<1$ **(M1)**. At $x=2$ we have $f''(2)=-12<0$, so it is concave on the middle interval $1<x<3$ **(A1)**. At $x=4$ we have $f''(4)=36>0$, so it is convex again on $x>3$ **(A1)**. The sign of $f''(x)$ alone decides the concavity on every open interval, and the integer test values keep the arithmetic exact and easy to verify.

**(d)** At $x=1$ the second derivative passes from positive to negative, and at $x=3$ it passes from negative to positive **(M1)**, so each of these points is a point of inflection **(A1)(AG)**. The function values at the two points are $f(1)=11$ and $f(3)=27$. A point of inflection is defined by a genuine change of sign in $f''(x)$, which occurs at both $x=1$ and $x=3$, and this is precisely why the classification is valid.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for the first derivative $4x^{3}-24x^{2}+36x$ and (A1) for the second derivative $12x^{2}-48x+36$. The factorisation (A1)(AG) requires $12(x-1)(x-3)$ to be shown; accept the working written in either order. A candidate who expands the bracket incorrectly loses the final mark but may keep the two derivative marks.

(b) Award (M1) for setting $12(x-1)(x-3)=0$ and (A1) for both roots $x=1$ and $x=3$. The remark that these are the only candidates is part of the reasoning and need not be written, but follow through from a wrong quadratic is allowed provided the solving step is consistent with it.

(c) Award (M1) for a correct sign test giving convex on $x<1$, (A1) for concave on $1<x<3$, and (A1) for convex on $x>3$. The three test values need not be $0$, $2$, $4$ but the computed signs must be correct. A candidate who states the concavity from $f'$ rather than $f''$ forfeits all three marks.

(d) Award (M1) for identifying the sign change at each root and (A1)(AG) for both points of inflection. The function values $11$ and $27$ are optional supporting detail; the decisive fact is the change of sign, and a candidate who states a root without showing the sign change earns at most one mark.
questions.explanation: The item is built around a quartic whose second derivative is a quadratic with two distinct real roots, so the student cannot treat the curve as having a single bending point. The first task is to differentiate twice and factor, which yields $f''(x)=12(x-1)(x-3)$. This factorisation is the spine of the whole question, because every later step depends on reading the two roots correctly from the brackets rather than from a sketch. The trap is to stop after finding $f''(x)=0$ and assume both roots are inflection points without checking the sign change, since a stationary point of the first derivative is not automatically an inflection. The intended route is to test one value in each of the three intervals $x<1$, $1<x<3$ and $x>3$, using the sign of $f''(x)$ to decide whether the curve is convex or concave. The values $0$, $2$ and $4$ are convenient because they give $36$, $-12$ and $36$, so the curve is convex, then concave, then convex again in that order. A point of inflection requires the second derivative to change sign, which it does at both $x=1$ and $x=3$, so both values qualify as inflection points. The classic error is to confuse a local minimum of $f'$ with an inflection, or to claim concavity from $f'$ instead of $f''$. Another common slip is to expand $12(x-1)(x-3)$ incorrectly and so miss one of the roots. The numbers were chosen so the second derivative is a clean quadratic and the test values are integers, which means a correct method produces exact signs while a mistaken factorisation usually does not.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.7 bullet on the second derivative, concavity and points of inflection. The lever is the quartic f(x) = x^4 - 8x^3 + 18x^2, whose second derivative is the quadratic 12x^2 - 48x + 36 = 12(x-1)(x-3); those coefficients were chosen so that the two real roots are the small integers 1 and 3, so that the three test values 0, 2 and 4 give the clean signs 36, minus 12 and 36, and so that the curve is convex, concave, convex in turn, making both roots genuine points of inflection rather than just stationary points. The item is not a reskin because the double root structure forces three interval tests and an explicit sign-change argument at two separate points, which a single-inflection question never requires.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the second derivative 12x^2 - 48x + 36 and its factorisation 12(x-1)(x-3), the two roots 1 and 3, the three test signs f''(0)=36, f''(2)=-12, f''(4)=36, and the function values f(1)=11 and f(3)=27.

questions.title: The cubic with a maximum and a minimum found by the second derivative
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.8 (local maximum and minimum points; use of f'(x)=0 and the second derivative test)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The cubic is written as a product of factors whose derivative gives two stationary points that must be classified by the second derivative test rather than read from a sketch.
questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$, which expands to $f(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By differentiating the expanded cubic form, show that $f'(x)=3(x-1)(x+1)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the stationary points of $f$, giving their $x$-coordinates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the second derivative $f''(x)=6x$ to classify each stationary point as a maximum or a minimum.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Differentiate the expanded form $f(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$ to obtain $f'(x)=3x^{2}-3$ **(M1)**. Factoring the result gives $3(x^{2}-1)=3(x-1)(x+1)$ **(A1)(AG)**. This matches the required derivative exactly, because the constant term $2$ disappears when the function is differentiated and the remaining terms factor neatly. The factorised form is the most useful version of the derivative, because it displays the roots directly without any further algebra.

**(b)** Stationary points occur where the gradient is zero, so solve $3(x-1)(x+1)=0$ **(M1)**. A product is zero when $x-1=0$ or $x+1=0$, giving the two $x$-coordinates $x=-1$ and $x=1$ **(A1)**. These are the only real solutions, so they are the complete list of places where the curve could turn. Both $x$-coordinates must be found before any classification can begin, since the second derivative test is applied separately at each one.

**(c)** The second derivative here is the simple linear function $f''(x)=6x$ **(M1)**. At $x=-1$ we have $f''(-1)=-6<0$, which means the curve is bending downwards, so the point is a local maximum **(A1)**. At $x=1$ we have $f''(1)=6>0$, which means the curve is bending upwards, so the point is a local minimum **(A1)**. This linear second derivative is unusually convenient, because its sign is fixed simply by the sign of $x$, and the sign of $f''$ alone decides the nature of each stationary point.

**(d)** Substitute the two $x$-values back into $f$. We have $f(-1)=(-1)^{3}-3(-1)+2=4$, so the local maximum is at $(-1,4)$ **(M1)(A1)**. Also $f(1)=1^{3}-3(1)+2=0$, so the local minimum is at $(1,0)$ **(A1)**. Recording both coordinates completes the description of the turning points and confirms the overall shape of the cubic, which is why the final coordinates are correct.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for the derivative $3x^{2}-3$ and (A1)(AG) for the factorised form $3(x-1)(x+1)$. Accept differentiation of the product $(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$ if it reaches the same result. A candidate who writes $3x^{2}-3$ but fails to factor it earns only the method mark and not the accuracy mark.

(b) Award (M1) for setting the derivative equal to zero and (A1) for both roots $x=-1$ and $x=1$. Follow through from an incorrect derivative is allowed provided the equation is solved consistently with it. Both roots are required for the later classification marks in part (c).

(c) Award (M1) for stating $f''(x)=6x$, (A1) for the local maximum at $x=-1$ using the fact that $f''(-1)<0$, and (A1) for the local minimum at $x=1$ using $f''(1)>0$. The second derivative test must actually be applied; a candidate who classifies from a sketch earns no credit here.

(d) Award (M1) for substituting into $f$ and (A1) for $(-1,4)$, then (A1) for $(1,0)$. A candidate who gives only the $x$-values forfeits the coordinate marks, and the values $4$ and $0$ must be computed, not read from a graph.
questions.explanation: The item is built on a cubic that is given in both factorised and expanded form, and the whole point is to classify two stationary points using the second derivative test. The derivative of $x^{3}-3x+2$ is $3x^{2}-3$, which factors as $3(x-1)(x+1)$, so the stationary points are at $x=-1$ and $x=1$. The second derivative is the unusually simple $6x$, and its signs at the two roots are opposite: $f''(-1)=-6<0$ marks a local maximum, while $f''(1)=6>0$ marks a local minimum. The trap is to infer the nature of the turning points from the shape of a cubic sketch, which is unreliable and is not what the syllabus asks for here; the second derivative test is the required route. The intended method is to compute $f''(x)$, evaluate it at each stationary point, and read the sign to decide maximum or minimum. The factorised and expanded forms together let a candidate verify their derivative two ways, which is a useful check against sign errors. The classic error is to mix up the two points and call $x=1$ the maximum, or to forget that the squared factor $(x-1)^{2}$ means $x=1$ is a repeated root of the derivative yet remains an ordinary minimum of the cubic. Another slip is to evaluate $f$ at the wrong root and swap the coordinates $4$ and $0$. The numbers were chosen so the second derivative is linear and the function values at the roots are the small integers $4$ and $0$, which means a correct method gives exact coordinates while a careless one usually swaps them.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.8 bullet on local maximum and minimum points and the use of f'(x)=0 with the second derivative test. The lever is the cubic f(x) = (x-1)^2(x+2) = x^3 - 3x + 2, whose derivative 3x^2 - 3 factors as 3(x-1)(x+1) to give stationary points at x = minus 1 and x = 1; those values were chosen so that the second derivative 6x is linear and gives opposite signs minus 6 and 6, so one point is a maximum and the other a minimum, and so that the function values at the roots are the clean integers 4 and 0. The item is not a reskin because the classification must come from the second derivative test rather than a sketch, and the squared factor tempts a candidate into misreading a stationary point of inflection.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the derivative 3x^2 - 3 and its factorisation 3(x-1)(x+1), the two roots minus 1 and 1, the second derivative 6x and its signs minus 6 and 6, and the function values f(-1)=4 and f(1)=0.

questions.title: The particle that stops twice and travels equal legs
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.9 (kinematic problems involving displacement s, velocity v and acceleration a)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The displacement is a cubic whose velocity factorises into two distinct roots, so the particle reverses direction twice and the total distance is not the net displacement.
questions.question: A particle moves along a line with displacement $s(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$ metres at time $t$ seconds, for $t\ge 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the velocity is $v(t)=3(t-1)(t-3)$ and that the acceleration is $a(t)=6t-12$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the times when the particle is at rest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the displacement of the particle at those times.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the total distance travelled by the particle in the interval $0\le t\le 4$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Differentiate the displacement with respect to time to get the velocity $v(t)=3t^{2}-12t+9$ **(M1)**, which factors as $3(t^{2}-4t+3)=3(t-1)(t-3)$ **(A1)(AG)**. Differentiate once more to obtain the acceleration $a(t)=6t-12$ **(A1)**. The velocity factorisation is exact, because expanding the bracket restores $3t^{2}-12t+9$, and this factored form makes the rest times immediate to read without solving a general quadratic.

**(b)** The particle is at rest when $v(t)=0$, so solve $3(t-1)(t-3)=0$ **(M1)**. This gives $t-1=0$ or $t-3=0$, hence the two times $t=1$ and $t=3$ **(A1)**. These are the only moments at which the velocity vanishes, so the direction of travel changes at both of these instants and the journey must be split there.

**(c)** Substitute each rest time into the displacement. At $t=1$ we have $s(1)=1-6+9=4$ **(M1)**, and at $t=3$ we have $s(3)=27-54+27=0$ **(A1)**. The displacements at the two stopping times are therefore $4$ m and $0$ m respectively, and the particle is momentarily stationary at each of these positions before it sets off again.

**(d)** Between $t=0$ and $t=4$ the particle moves from $s(0)=0$ out to $s(1)=4$, back to $s(3)=0$, then out again to $s(4)=4$ **(M1)**. The three legs each have length $|4-0|=4$, $|0-4|=4$ and $|4-0|=4$ **(A1)**, so the total distance is $4+4+4=12$ m **(A1)**. Summing the absolute leg lengths is the only correct way to measure the path actually travelled, and the distinction between total distance and net displacement is the central idea tested here, so the total path length is the sum of three separate four-metre legs, which is why it equals $12$ and not the net displacement of $4$.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for the velocity $3t^{2}-12t+9$, (A1)(AG) for the factorised velocity $3(t-1)(t-3)$, and (A1) for the acceleration $a(t)=6t-12$. A candidate who differentiates only once and states the wrong acceleration loses the last mark but keeps the velocity marks if the differentiation is otherwise correct.

(b) Award (M1) for solving $v(t)=0$ and (A1) for both times $t=1$ and $t=3$. Follow through from an incorrect velocity factorisation is allowed if the solving is consistent with it. Both rest times are needed for the distance in part (d).

(c) Award (M1) for substituting into $s(t)$ and (A1) for the pair of displacements $4$ and $0$. The order is important: $s(1)=4$ and $s(3)=0$. A candidate who swaps the two values earns at most one mark.

(d) Award (M1) for identifying the four positional values $0$, $4$, $0$, $4$, (A1) for the three leg lengths each equal to $4$, and (A1) for the total $12$. A candidate who reports the net displacement $4$ instead of the total distance forfeits the final marks. The absolute values are essential to the method.
questions.explanation: The item is built on a kinematic cubic whose velocity has two distinct roots, so the particle stops and turns around twice within the interval. The displacement is $s(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$, whose derivative is $v(t)=3t^{2}-12t+9=3(t-1)(t-3)$, and the acceleration is $a(t)=6t-12$. The rest times are therefore $t=1$ and $t=3$, and the displacements there are $s(1)=4$ and $s(3)=0$. The trap, and the heart of the question, is that total distance is not the net displacement: between $t=0$ and $t=4$ the particle travels out to $4$, returns to $0$, and goes out again to $4$, so each leg is $4$ m and the total is $12$ m, whereas the net displacement from start to finish is only $4$ m. The intended route is to split the journey at the rest times, take the absolute value of each leg, and add them together. Splitting at the rest times is the only reliable way to capture the reversal, because a single displacement difference assumes monotonic motion throughout. The equal leg lengths are a direct consequence of the symmetric roots of the velocity, and they make the total distance an obvious multiple of one leg. The classic error is to compute $s(4)-s(0)=4$ and call that the distance travelled, which ignores the reversal completely. Another slip is to evaluate the acceleration at the rest times, $a(1)=-6$ and $a(3)=6$, and confuse its sign with the direction of motion. The numbers were chosen so the three legs are equal and integer, giving a clean total of $12$, while a candidate who omits the absolute values usually reports $4$ and fails the final part.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.9 bullet on kinematic problems involving displacement, velocity and acceleration. The lever is the displacement s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t, whose velocity 3t^2 - 12t + 9 factors as 3(t-1)(t-3) to give two rest times t = 1 and t = 3; those values were chosen so that the displacements at rest are 4 and 0, so that the particle travels three equal legs of 4 m each, and so that the total distance 12 m differs strikingly from the net displacement 4 m. The item is not a reskin because the reversal of direction twice forces an absolute-value sum of legs rather than a single net-displacement subtraction, and the equal legs expose the common error of reporting the net displacement as the distance.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the velocity factorisation 3(t-1)(t-3) at t=1 and t=3 giving zero, the displacements s(1)=4 and s(3)=0, the accelerations a(1)=-6 and a(3)=6, and the total distance as the sum of absolute legs 4+4+4=12.

questions.title: The indefinite integral that needs a logarithm and a cosine
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.10 (indefinite integral of x^n, n in Q, sin x, cos x, 1/x, e^x)
questions.subtopic: 5.10 Indefinite integral of x^n, sin x, cos x, 1/x, e^x
questions.challenge_mechanism: The integrand mixes a power, a reciprocal, an exponential and a sine, so the antiderivative must combine a logarithm with a cosine and then be pinned by an initial value.
questions.question: Find the indefinite integral $\int\left(3x^{2}-\frac{2}{x}+6\mathrm{e}^{x}-4\sin x\right)\mathrm{d}x$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the general antiderivative, including the constant of integration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the derivative of your answer and confirm that it returns the original integrand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value of the antiderivative at $x=1$, taking the constant of integration to be zero.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the constant of integration if the antiderivative takes the value $7$ when $x=1$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Integrate the expression term by term, because the integral of a sum is the sum of the separate integrals. The power term gives $\int 3x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x=x^{3}$ **(M1)**. The reciprocal term gives $\int -\frac{2}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=-2\ln|x|$ **(A1)**, where the absolute value is required so the logarithm is defined. The exponential term gives $\int 6\mathrm{e}^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and the sine term gives $\int -4\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x=4\cos x$ **(A1)**, since the derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$. No term affects another, so the four rules can be applied in any order, and adding the constant of integration gives the general antiderivative $F(x)=x^{3}-2\ln|x|+6\mathrm{e}^{x}+4\cos x+C$ **(A1)(AG)**. Each standard rule is applied to one term independently, so the final result is the sum of four antiderivatives.

**(b)** Differentiate the answer to check it. We have $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x^{3})=3x^{2}$ **(M1)**, $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(-2\ln|x|)=-\frac{2}{x}$ **(A1)**, $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(6\mathrm{e}^{x})=6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(4\cos x)=-4\sin x$ **(A1)**. Adding these derivatives gives exactly the original integrand $3x^{2}-\frac{2}{x}+6\mathrm{e}^{x}-4\sin x$ **(A1)(AG)**. This reverse check is valuable, because it catches any single sign slip instantly, and the derivative undoes the integration term by term, which is why the check confirms the antiderivative is correct.

**(c)** With $C=0$ and $x=1$, substitute to obtain $F(1)=1-2\ln 1+6\mathrm{e}^{1}+4\cos 1$ **(M1)**. Because $\ln 1=0$, this simplifies to $1+6\mathrm{e}+4\cos 1$, which evaluates to $19.470900$ to six decimal places **(A1)**. The logarithm contributes nothing at $x=1$, so the value is dominated by the exponential and the cosine term, and those two terms together account for almost the whole magnitude of the result.

**(d)** The condition $F(1)=7$ gives $19.470900+C=7$ **(M1)**, so the constant is $C=7-19.470900=-12.470900$ **(A1)(AG)**. This constant shifts the whole antiderivative downwards so that its graph passes through the point $(1,7)$. Choosing the constant in this way fixes a unique member of the family of antiderivatives, and the negative sign is required because the value without the constant already exceeds $7$, which is why $C$ must be negative.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for integrating the power term to $x^{3}$ and (A1) for $-2\ln|x|$; the absolute value bars are required for full credit. Award (A1) for $6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and (A1) for $4\cos x$, noting the sign change that comes from integrating $-4\sin x$. The final (A1)(AG) is for the combined antiderivative $x^{3}-2\ln|x|+6\mathrm{e}^{x}+4\cos x+C$. A candidate who writes $\ln x$ without bars earns the term mark only, not full credit.

(b) Award (M1) for the derivative of the power term and (A1) for $-2/x$ from the logarithm. Award (A1) for $6\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and (A1) for $-4\sin x$, with (A1)(AG) for recovery of the original integrand. The confirmation must show the derivative equals the given integrand term by term.

(c) Award (M1) for substituting $x=1$ with $C=0$ and (A1) for the numerical value $19.470900$ to six decimal places. Accept $19.47$ if rounded, but the exact form $1+6\mathrm{e}+4\cos 1$ is preferred in the markscheme.

(d) Award (M1) for forming $19.470900+C=7$ and (A1)(AG) for $C=-12.470900$. Follow through from an incorrect part (c) value is allowed provided the subtraction is consistent with it. A candidate who misses the negative sign earns no credit for the final answer.
questions.explanation: The item is built on the indefinite integral of a sum that deliberately spans four different standard forms: a power, a reciprocal, an exponential and a sine. The antiderivative must combine a logarithm with a cosine, because integrating $-2/x$ gives $-2\ln|x|$ and integrating $-4\sin x$ gives $+4\cos x$, since the derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$. Combining a logarithm and a cosine in one antiderivative is unusual enough that candidates often second-guess the sign of the cosine term. The trap is to mishandle one of these signs, most often writing $-4\cos x$ instead of $+4\cos x$, or dropping the absolute value on the logarithm. Part (b) is the built-in self-check: differentiating the answer must return the integrand term by term, and it exposes any sign error at once. The evaluation at $x=1$ is chosen because $\ln 1$ vanishes, isolating the exponential and cosine contributions, so the value is $1+6\mathrm{e}+4\cos 1\approx 19.470900$. Part (d) then pins the curve by requiring $F(1)=7$, so $C=7-19.470900=-12.470900$, and requiring an initial condition turns the family of antiderivatives into a single curve. The classic error is to integrate $-4\sin x$ as $-4\cos x$, which fails the part (b) check, or to forget that $\ln 1=0$ and keep an erroneous constant term. The numbers were chosen so the part (c) value is not an integer, forcing a calculator evaluation, while the part (d) constant is a clean subtraction from it. The interplay of the four forms is the point of the exercise, and the logarithm-plus-cosine combination is the feature most likely to be mis-remembered under pressure. A calculator is genuinely needed only at the final numerical evaluation, since every algebraic step is exact.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.10 bullet on the indefinite integral of x^n, sin x, cos x, 1/x and e^x. The lever is the integrand 3x^2 - 2/x + 6e^x - 4 sin x, which mixes four standard forms so that the antiderivative must contain both a logarithm and a cosine; those coefficients were chosen so that the power integrates to x^3, the reciprocal to minus 2 ln|x|, the exponential to 6e^x and the sine to plus 4 cos x, and so that evaluating at x = 1 gives 1 + 6e + 4 cos 1 is approximately 19.470900, from which the initial condition F(1) = 7 yields the clean constant minus 12.470900. The item is not a reskin because the four-form mix forces a sign-sensitive logarithm-plus-cosine antiderivative and then an initial-value correction, which a single-form integral never requires.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the antiderivative x^3 - 2 ln|x| + 6 e^x + 4 cos x + C, its derivative returning the integrand, the value at x=1 with C=0 as 1 - 2 ln 1 + 6e + 4 cos 1 = 19.470900, the adjusted value 19.470900 - 12.470900 = 7, and the checks 6e^0 = 6 and -4 sin 0 = 0.

questions.title: The area trapped between a parabola and a line
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.11 (definite integrals, including analytical approach to areas between curves)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The region is bounded by a parabola and a line whose intersection gives two limits, and the area is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower over that interval.
questions.question: The region $R$ is bounded by the parabola $y=x^{2}-4$ and the line $y=2x-1$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the two curves intersect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the line $y=2x-1$ is the upper curve on the interval between the intersection points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the total area enclosed by the two curves.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the area of the part of the region with $x\ge 0$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Set the two curves equal: $x^{2}-4=2x-1$ rearranges to $x^{2}-2x-3=0$ **(M1)**. Factoring gives $(x-3)(x+1)=0$, so the intersection $x$-coordinates are $x=-1$ and $x=3$ **(A1)(AG)**. Solving the quadratic is the necessary first step, because the limits of the area integral are exactly these $x$-values, and no other points bound the enclosed region between the two graphs.

**(b)** On the interval $[-1,3]$ compare the curves at a test point, for example $x=0$: the line gives $2(0)-1=-1$ while the parabola gives $0^{2}-4=-4$ **(M1)**. Since $-1>-4$, the line lies above the parabola **(A1)**. Equivalently the difference $(2x-1)-(x^{2}-4)=-x^{2}+2x+3=-(x-3)(x+1)$ is non-negative on $[-1,3]$ **(A1)(AG)**. Confirming the upper curve matters, since integrating the lower minus the upper would give a negative result, and the non-negativity of the difference on the whole interval removes any doubt about which curve to subtract.

**(c)** The area is $\int_{-1}^{3}[(2x-1)-(x^{2}-4)]\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_{-1}^{3}(-x^{2}+2x+3)\,\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)**. The antiderivative is $-\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}+3x$ **(A1)**, so evaluating gives $\left(-9+9+9\right)-\left(\frac{1}{3}+1-3\right)=9-\left(-\frac{5}{3}\right)=\frac{32}{3}$ **(A1)**. The antiderivative is a simple cubic, so only arithmetic remains once the setup is correct, and the positive value confirms the orientation of the integration was chosen properly, which is why the answer is $\frac{32}{3}$.

**(d)** For the part with $x\ge 0$ the region runs from $0$ to $3$, so the area is $\int_{0}^{3}(-x^{2}+2x+3)\,\mathrm{d}x$ **(M1)**. Using the same antiderivative gives $\left(-9+9+9\right)-0=9$ **(A1)(AG)**. Restricting to $x$ at least zero simply changes the lower limit and leaves the integrand unchanged, and this sub-region is a clean integer, which makes the comparison with the full area instructive, so the area is exactly $9$ and not the full $\frac{32}{3}$.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for forming the equation $x^{2}-2x-3=0$ and (A1)(AG) for the roots $x=-1$ and $x=3$. A candidate who solves correctly but writes the factors wrongly earns at most the method mark.

(b) Award (M1) for a comparison at a test point or for writing the difference expression, (A1) for concluding the line is above the parabola, and (A1)(AG) for showing the difference $-(x-3)(x+1)$ is non-negative on $[-1,3]$. A sketch alone is not enough; the inequality must be justified algebraically or numerically.

(c) Award (M1) for setting up the integral of upper minus lower, (A1) for the antiderivative $-\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}+3x$, and (A1) for the value $\frac{32}{3}$. The subtraction at the lower limit must give $9-(-5/3)$; a candidate who forgets to subtract the lower value forfeits the final mark. The arithmetic $-5/3$ at the lower limit is the step most often dropped.

(d) Award (M1) for the integral from $0$ to $3$ and (A1)(AG) for the value $9$. Follow through from an incorrect part (c) integrand is allowed if the working is consistent. A candidate who integrates from $-1$ to $0$ instead of $0$ to $3$ earns no credit for this part.
questions.explanation: The item is built on the area between two curves, where the limits of integration come from the intersection of a parabola and a line. Setting $x^{2}-4=2x-1$ gives $x^{2}-2x-3=0$, which factors as $(x-3)(x+1)=0$, so the curves meet at $x=-1$ and $x=3$. The trap is to integrate the parabola minus the line, or to skip the check of which curve is on top; on $[-1,3]$ the line $y=2x-1$ lies above the parabola, because their difference $-x^{2}+2x+3=-(x-3)(x+1)$ is non-negative between the roots. The intended route is to integrate upper minus lower: $\int_{-1}^{3}(-x^{2}+2x+3)\,\mathrm{d}x$, whose antiderivative is $-\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x^{2}+3x$, giving $9-(-5/3)=32/3$. Part (d) then asks only for the right-hand portion with $x\ge 0$, which is $\int_{0}^{3}$ of the same integrand and equals $9$. Establishing the upper curve by the sign of the difference is the key step, because reversing the subtraction produces a negative area that no absolute value can later fix. The classic error is to use the wrong lower limit in part (d) by integrating from $-1$ to $0$, or to forget to subtract the antiderivative at the lower limit and write $9$ for the whole region instead of $32/3$. Another slip is to treat the two curves as if they cross again inside the interval. The numbers were chosen so the intersection roots are small integers and the two areas are the clean fractions $32/3$ and $9$, so a correct method produces exact values while a sign error does not. The clean integer sub-region makes the contrast with the full fractional area especially clear.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.11 bullet on definite integrals and the analytical approach to areas between curves. The lever is the region bounded by the parabola y = x^2 - 4 and the line y = 2x - 1; those equations were chosen so that equating them gives x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0 = (x-3)(x+1), yielding intersection limits minus 1 and 3, so that the upper curve is the line with a clean non-negative difference, and so that the total area is 32/3 while the right-hand portion with x at least 0 is exactly 9. The item is not a reskin because it requires establishing which curve is upper by sign of the difference and then computing a sub-region area from a shifted lower limit, which a single-curve area question never demands.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the intersection equation x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0 with roots minus 1 and 3, the antiderivative -x^3/3 + x^2 + 3x evaluated at 3 giving 9 and at minus 1 giving minus 5/3, the total area 9 - (-5/3) = 32/3, and the right-hand area from 0 to 3 giving 9.
